name: Millerite revival context
description: Millerism emerged during the Second Great Awakening.
narrative: Millerism emerged during the Second Great Awakening. Miller’s reading of Daniel led him to expect a literal return of Christ in the 1840s. Public lectures, Himes’s publishing work, and camp meetings carried the message across denominational lines. The failed expectations of 1844 produced deep disappointment and competing explanations. Some followers abandoned the movement; others reorganized into distinct Adventist traditions. It was a revival network rather than a single church that formally dissolved on one date.

key_figures.name: William Miller
key_figures.summary: A Baptist preacher and prophetic interpreter whose expectation of Christ’s near return drew an interdenominational revival following.

key_figures.name: Joshua V. Himes
key_figures.role: publisher and organizer who expanded the revival’s reach
key_figures.summary: An Adventist organizer and publisher who greatly expanded Miller’s audience and later worked to sustain Adventist cooperation after the 1844 disappointment.

name: Advent Christian formation
description: Advent Christian Church organized in 1860 within the Adventist stream.
narrative: Advent Christian Church organized in 1860 within the Adventist stream. Advent Christians developed within the post-Millerite search for a sustainable Advent witness, organizing in the nineteenth century rather than adopting the Sabbatarian Adventist system. The existing 1860 date marks organizational origins. Their identity joins evangelical faith with conditional immortality and the expectation of Christ’s return. Contemporary statements must be checked for adoption status: the proposed 2026 Declaration of Principles did not receive the required vote.

name: SDA organization
narrative: Seventh-day Adventist Church organized in 1863. Sabbatarian believers emerging from the Millerite disappointment gradually developed a common identity, publications, and organization. The General Conference was organized in Battle Creek in May 1863. The resulting denomination combined mission, education, and health work with distinctive interpretation of the Sabbath and heavenly sanctuary. Its current beliefs reflect development beyond the original Millerite coalition, not an unchanged creed carried intact from 1844.

name: Sabbatarian Adventist separation
description: Sabbatarian Adventists separated in 1858, forming the line later known as Church of God (Seventh Day).
narrative: Sabbatarian Adventists separated in 1858, forming the line later known as Church of God (Seventh Day). The church traces its development to believers in western Michigan in 1858. It grew within the Sabbatarian Adventist environment while developing separately from the denomination that became Seventh-day Adventist. Publishing and later conference organization sustained the fellowship. This node refers principally to the General Conference tradition; similarly named Church of God bodies are not automatically the same organization.
